title: PHY_108 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: A spring is loaded and its extension e is plotted against the load m. The best-fit line passes through (0.20 kg, 4.5 cm) and (0.80 kg, 13.5 cm). Find the gradient and the y-intercept.
questions.concept: Gradient and intercept of a best-fit line
questions.why:
Gradient m = (13.5 − 4.5)/(0.80 − 0.20) = 9.0/0.60 = 15.0 cm/kg. Then c = y − mx at either point: 4.5 − 15.0(0.20) = 1.5 cm, the extension the line predicts at zero load.

9.0 cm/kg takes the rise in e without dividing by the change in load; 4.5 cm quotes the first point's y-value as the intercept instead of going back to m = 0; 0.067 kg/cm is Δx/Δy, the reciprocal of the gradient.

questions.q: A cooling curve is plotted as temperature θ against time t. The best-fit line has gradient −2.5 °C/min and cuts the θ-axis at 60 °C. At what time does the line predict θ = 0?
questions.concept: x-intercept of a straight-line graph
questions.why:
For y = mx + c the x-intercept comes from setting y = 0: 0 = mx + c, so x = −c/m = −60/(−2.5) = 24 min.

−24 min drops the minus sign that the negative gradient supplies, giving a time before the start; 150 min multiplies c by m instead of dividing; 0.042 min is m/c, the reciprocal of the correct ratio.

questions.q: A power law y = kxⁿ is tested by plotting log₁₀ y against log₁₀ x. The best-fit line passes through (0.40, 0.86) and (1.60, 2.66). Find n and k.
questions.concept: Power-law linearisation on a log-log plot
questions.why:
Taking logs, log y = n log x + log k, so the gradient is n and the intercept is log k. n = (2.66 − 0.86)/(1.60 − 0.40) = 1.80/1.20 = 1.5. Intercept log k = 0.86 − 1.5(0.40) = 0.26, so k = 10^0.26 = 1.82.

k = 0.26 reads the intercept as k without undoing the logarithm; n = 0.67 is Δx/Δy, the reciprocal gradient; k = 7.24 is 10^0.86, using the first point's y-value instead of the intercept.

questions.q: Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂/r² is tested with two equal charges q. A plot of F against 1/r² is a straight line through the origin of gradient 0.045 N·m². Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². Find q.
questions.concept: Linearised Coulomb's law: gradient of F against 1/r²
questions.why:
Written as F = (kq₁q₂)(1/r²), the plot of F against 1/r² has gradient kq₁q₂ = kq². So q² = 0.045/(9.0 × 10⁹) = 5.0 × 10⁻¹² C², and q = √(5.0 × 10⁻¹²) = 2.24 × 10⁻⁶ C = 2.24 μC.

5.00 × 10⁻¹² C quotes q² as if it were q, missing the square root; 1.12 μC halves the answer, as if the two equal charges shared it; 2.24 × 10⁻⁵ C is the right figure with the decimal point moved one place.

questions.q: The true thickness of a beam is 4.80 mm and a student measures it as 4.62 mm. Give the percentage error and the percentage difference of the measured value from the true value.
questions.concept: Percentage error and percentage difference
questions.why:
Actual error = |4.80 − 4.62| = 0.18 mm. Percentage error = (0.18/4.80) × 100 = 3.75 %, quoted as a magnitude. Percentage difference = (observed − reference)/reference × 100 = (4.62 − 4.80)/4.80 × 100 = −3.75 %, and it keeps its sign because the measured value is below the true one.

+3.75 % throws away the sign that percentage difference must carry; 3.90 % divides by the measured value instead of the true value; 0.0375 % loses the factor of 100.

questions.q: A mass on a spring obeys T = 2π√(m/k). Readings: m = 0.20 kg gives T = 0.89 s, and m = 0.80 kg gives T = 1.78 s. Both points lie on the best-fit line of T² against m. Find the spring constant k.
questions.concept: Spring constant from a T² against m graph
questions.why:
Square first: T² = 0.792 s² and 3.168 s². Gradient = (3.168 − 0.792)/(0.80 − 0.20) = 2.376/0.60 = 3.96 s²/kg. Since T² = (4π²/k)m, the gradient equals 4π²/k, so k = 4π²/3.96 = 39.48/3.96 = 9.97 N/m.

3.96 N/m stops at the gradient and calls it k; 156 N/m multiplies by 4π² instead of dividing; 1.48 N/m uses T instead of T² on the y-axis.

questions.q: A rectangle is measured as 12.3 cm by 4.0 cm. Give its area to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.concept: Significant figures in a computed result
questions.why:
12.3 × 4.0 = 49.2 cm². In a product the answer carries the number of significant figures of the least precise factor: 4.0 has two, so the area is quoted to two significant figures as 49 cm².

49.2 cm² keeps three figures, claiming precision the 4.0 cm reading does not have; 49.20 cm² keeps four; 50 cm² rounds to one figure, which throws away a figure that was measured.

questions.q: The relation v² = u² + 2as links final speed v to distance s, with the initial speed u and the acceleration a both constant. Which plot gives a straight line, and what do its gradient and intercept equal?
options: Plot v against s: gradient a, intercept u
Plot v² against s²: gradient 2a, intercept u²
Plot s against v²: gradient 2a, intercept u²
Plot v² against s: gradient 2a, intercept u²
questions.concept: Choosing the plot that linearises a relation
questions.why:
Compare v² = (2a)s + u² with y = mx + c. The y-variable must be v², the x-variable s, so the gradient is 2a and the intercept is u².

Plotting v against s leaves the squared term in place, so the graph curves; v² against s² squares a variable that is already linear; s against v² swaps the axes, which turns the gradient into 1/(2a) and the intercept into −u²/(2a).

questions.q: A faulty instrument pushes every reading on the y-axis up by the same fixed amount. What happens to the straight line drawn through the plotted points?
options: The intercept changes; the gradient is unchanged
The gradient changes; the intercept is unchanged
Both the gradient and the intercept change
Neither the gradient nor the intercept changes
questions.concept: Effect of a systematic error on a graph
questions.why:
Adding a constant to every y-value shifts the whole line bodily upward. Differences between y-values are untouched, so (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) is the same as before and the gradient survives; only the value of y at x = 0 moves, so the intercept carries the whole of the fault.

This is why a physical quantity is extracted from a gradient wherever possible, and why an intercept that should be zero is the standard test for a systematic error. A random error would scatter points about the line rather than displace it.

questions.q:
Readings for a resistor of nominal value 2.2 kΩ:
V (V): 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00
I (mA): 0.22, 0.45, 0.68, 0.91
The best-fit line of V against I passes through the first and last points. Find R in ohms and the percentage error.
questions.concept: Resistance from the gradient of a V against I graph
questions.why:
Gradient = (2.00 − 0.50)/(0.91 − 0.22) = 1.50/0.69 = 2.17 V/mA. Because the current axis is in milliamperes, that gradient is 2.17 kΩ, so R = 2174 Ω. Percentage error = |2174 − 2200|/2200 × 100 = 1.2 %, inside the 5 % the experiment accepts.

2.17 Ω forgets the milliampere-to-ampere conversion and is out by a factor of 1000; 2273 Ω uses V/I at the first point alone instead of the gradient of the whole line; 460 Ω is the reciprocal gradient, 0.69/1.50, read as a resistance.

questions.q: A 6.0 Ω and a 12.0 Ω resistor are joined in parallel, and that combination is in series with a 4.0 Ω resistor across a 10 V supply. Find the total resistance and the current drawn from the supply.
questions.concept: Series and parallel resistor networks
questions.why:
For the parallel pair, R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = (6.0 × 12.0)/18.0 = 4.0 Ω, which is smaller than the smaller resistor, as it must be. Adding the series 4.0 Ω gives 8.0 Ω, and I = V/R = 10/8.0 = 1.25 A.

22.0 Ω adds all three in series; 2.0 Ω puts all three in parallel; 13.0 Ω averages the parallel pair as (6 + 12)/2 = 9 Ω instead of using the reciprocal formula.

questions.q: Two resistors give 8.0 Ω when joined in series and 1.5 Ω when joined in parallel. What are the two resistances?
questions.concept: Finding two resistors from their series and parallel values
questions.why:
In series R₁ + R₂ = 8.0. In parallel R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 1.5, so R₁R₂ = 1.5 × 8.0 = 12. The two numbers are the roots of x² − 8x + 12 = 0, which factorises as (x − 2)(x − 6), giving 2.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω. Check: 2 + 6 = 8 and (2 × 6)/8 = 1.5.

3.0 Ω and 5.0 Ω sum correctly but give a parallel value of 15/8 = 1.875 Ω; 1.5 Ω and 6.5 Ω simply copy the parallel value into one branch; 4.0 Ω and 4.0 Ω sum correctly but give 2.0 Ω in parallel.

questions.q: A resistance is to be found from paired current and potential-difference readings. Which arrangement of the two meters is correct?
options: Ammeter in series with the resistor, voltmeter in parallel across it
Ammeter in parallel across the resistor, voltmeter in series with it
Both meters in series with the resistor
Both meters in parallel across the resistor
questions.concept: Meter connection in a V and I measurement
questions.why:
An ammeter reads the current that passes through it, so it must be in the same path as the resistor, in series, and is built with a very low resistance so it barely changes that current. A voltmeter reads the difference in potential between two points, so it must be connected across those two points, in parallel, and is built with a very high resistance so it barely diverts current.

Swapping them puts a low resistance across the resistor, short-circuiting it, and a high resistance in the path, choking the current to almost nothing.

questions.q: A student plots I in milliamperes on the y-axis against V in volts on the x-axis for a fixed resistor. The best-fit line passes through the origin with gradient 0.40. What is the resistance in ohms?
questions.concept: Resistance from the gradient of an I against V graph
questions.why:
With I on the y-axis the gradient is I/V = 1/R, not R. Here 0.40 mA/V = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ A/V, so R = 1/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2500 Ω, that is 2.5 kΩ.

0.40 Ω reads the gradient straight off as a resistance; 2.5 Ω takes the reciprocal but leaves the current in milliamperes, so the answer is out by 1000; 400 Ω multiplies the gradient by 1000 instead of inverting it.

questions.q: You are given two 100 Ω resistors and one 50 Ω resistor, and must use all three. What are the largest and the smallest resistances you can obtain?
questions.concept: Largest and smallest resistance from three resistors
questions.why:
All three in series gives the largest value, 100 + 100 + 50 = 250 Ω. All three in parallel gives the smallest: 1/R = 1/100 + 1/100 + 1/50 = 0.01 + 0.01 + 0.02 = 0.04, so R = 25 Ω, below the smallest single resistor as it must be.

50 Ω puts only the two equal resistors in parallel and forgets the third; 200 Ω leaves the 50 Ω out of the series total; 33.3 Ω treats all three as 100 Ω and quotes 100/3.

questions.q:
Two components are tested over the same range:
A: V (V) 2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0 with I (mA) 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0
B: V (V) 2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0 with I (mA) 0.8, 2.0, 4.2, 7.5
Which component is ohmic, and what is its resistance?
questions.concept: Identifying an ohmic component from a V and I table
questions.why:
Test each row for a constant V/I. For A: 2.0/1.0 = 2.0, 4.0/2.0 = 2.0, 6.0/3.0 = 2.0, 8.0/4.0 = 2.0, all in kΩ, so A is ohmic with R = 2.0 kΩ. For B the ratio falls from 2.5 kΩ to 1.07 kΩ, so B is non-ohmic and has no single resistance.

0.5 kΩ is I/V for A rather than V/I; the two answers naming B quote its ratio at one end of the range, but a value that changes across the table is exactly what disqualifies it.

questions.q: Why must the voltmeter used to measure the potential difference across a resistor have a very high resistance?
options: So it can survive a large potential difference
So it responds quickly to a changing reading
So it draws almost no current from the part it is connected across
So it can be connected in series without altering the current
questions.concept: Why a voltmeter has a high resistance
questions.why:
The voltmeter sits in parallel with the component, so it offers a second path for current. The current it takes is V divided by its own resistance; making that resistance very large makes the diverted current negligible, so the circuit is left as it was and the reading is the true potential difference.

Withstanding a large voltage is a matter of insulation, not resistance; speed of response is a mechanical property of the movement; and a voltmeter is never placed in series, where its high resistance would nearly stop the current.

questions.q: For an iron resistor, the graph of P against I² is a straight line of gradient 47.6 Ω. The resistor is marked 50 Ω. What is the percentage error in the value obtained from the graph?
questions.concept: Percentage error of a resistance from a P against I² graph
questions.why:
Comparing P = RI² with y = mx + c, the gradient is R, so the experimental value is 47.6 Ω. Percentage error = |accepted − experimental|/accepted × 100 = |50 − 47.6|/50 × 100 = (2.4/50) × 100 = 4.8 %.

5.0 % divides by the experimental value instead of the accepted one; 2.4 % quotes the absolute error in ohms as though it were a percentage; 0.048 % loses the factor of 100.

questions.q:
A conductor is expected to obey P = I²R with R constant. The recorded rows are:
I (A): 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60
P (W): 1.00, 2.25, 4.00, 7.50, 9.00
Which row should be re-taken?
questions.concept: Spotting a reading that breaks P = I²R
questions.why:
Divide each P by I² to test for a constant R: 1.00/0.04 = 25, 2.25/0.09 = 25, 4.00/0.16 = 25, 7.50/0.25 = 30, 9.00/0.36 = 25. Four rows give 25 Ω and one gives 30 Ω, so the row at I = 0.50 A is the odd one; on the P against I² plot it is the single point off the line. The value the line predicts there is 25 × 0.25 = 6.25 W.

The other three rows all sit exactly on the line of gradient 25 Ω and give no reason to be repeated.

questions.q: A filament lamp is marked 240 V, 60 W, and its resistance when cold is 80 Ω. Find its resistance at its working point and the current that flows at the instant it is switched on.
questions.concept: Operating resistance and switch-on current of a lamp
questions.why:
At the working point P = V²/R, so R = V²/P = 240²/60 = 57600/60 = 960 Ω. At the instant of switching on the filament is still cold at 80 Ω, so I = V/R = 240/80 = 3.0 A, twelve times the running current of 60/240 = 0.25 A. That surge is why lamp filaments usually fail as they are switched on.

4.0 Ω comes from V/P instead of V²/P; 0.25 A is the running current, which flows only once the filament is hot; 80 Ω with 0.25 A mixes the cold resistance with the hot current.

questions.q: On the I against V curve for a tungsten filament, the tangent drawn at one point has slope 0.025 A/V. What is the resistance of the filament at that point?
questions.concept: Resistance from the tangent to an I against V curve
questions.why:
With I on the y-axis and V on the x-axis, the slope is I/V, which is 1/R at that point. So R = 1/0.025 = 40 Ω. The curve bends because this slope changes from point to point, which is the whole result of the experiment.

0.025 Ω reads the slope itself as a resistance; 25 Ω multiplies the slope by 1000, as if the current had been in milliamperes; 400 Ω inverts correctly but then shifts the decimal point one place.

questions.q:
A tungsten resistor gives:
V (V): 5.0, 10.0, 20.0
I (A): 0.50, 0.80, 1.00
Find its resistance at the lowest and at the highest reading, and say what the change shows.
options: 10.0 Ω and 20.0 Ω, so the resistance rises as the filament heats
10.0 Ω and 20.0 Ω, so the resistance falls as the filament heats
0.10 Ω and 0.05 Ω, so the resistance falls as the filament heats
10.0 Ω and 12.5 Ω, so the resistance stays constant
questions.concept: Resistance of a filament at two operating points
questions.why:
R = V/I at each reading: 5.0/0.50 = 10.0 Ω, 10.0/0.80 = 12.5 Ω and 20.0/1.00 = 20.0 Ω. The resistance doubles from the lowest to the highest reading. The current heats the filament through P = I²R, the temperature rises, and a metal's resistance rises with temperature, so the current stops growing in step with the voltage and the I against V graph curves over.

Saying the resistance falls contradicts the numbers; 0.10 Ω and 0.05 Ω are I/V rather than V/I; the last option quotes the middle reading and then denies the change it shows.

questions.q: For an iron resistor, the P against I² graph is a straight line through (0.09 A², 2.25 W) and (0.49 A², 12.25 W). Find the gradient and the current at which the resistor would dissipate 20.0 W.
questions.concept: Gradient of a P against I² graph and the current for a given power
questions.why:
Gradient = (12.25 − 2.25)/(0.49 − 0.09) = 10.00/0.40 = 25.0, and since P = RI² the gradient is the resistance, 25.0 Ω. For 20.0 W, I² = P/R = 20.0/25.0 = 0.800 A², so I = √0.800 = 0.894 A.

0.800 A stops at I² and never takes the square root; 0.040 Ω is the reciprocal gradient; 50.0 Ω doubles the gradient, as if the graph had been P against 2I².

questions.q: The graph of P against I² for a conductor is accepted as verifying Joule's law only if it passes through the origin. What makes the origin compulsory?
options: Power is proportional to the voltage
The resistance is constant over the range
questions.concept: Why the P against I² line passes through the origin
questions.why:
P = I²R has no constant term, so when I = 0 the power must be 0: y = mx with c = 0. A line of the right gradient but a clear non-zero intercept therefore reports power being dissipated with no current flowing, which is impossible, and signals a systematic fault such as a meter zero error or a stray offset in the recorded values.

A constant resistance makes the line straight but says nothing about where it cuts the axis; power is proportional to I² here, not to V alone; and the ammeter's resistance affects the size of the current, not the position of the origin.

questions.q: In the tungsten and iron resistor experiment, which listed effect is the one the experiment is designed to display rather than to remove?
options: Parallax when reading the ammeter scale
Drift of the supply between setting the voltage and recording
questions.concept: Sources of error in the non-ohmic resistor experiment
questions.why:
The whole point of the experiment is that the current heats the conductor, the temperature rises, the resistance changes with it, and the I against V graph bends. Self-heating is therefore the effect under study, not a fault, which is why readings are spread over the full 0.1 V to 50 V range where the bending is strongest.

Parallax, a voltmeter zero error and supply drift are genuine faults that add scatter or a systematic shift and should be reduced by reading squarely, zeroing the meter and letting the setting settle before recording.

questions.q: Five wires meet at a junction. Two carry 4.20 mA and 1.35 mA into it, and two carry 2.60 mA and 0.95 mA out of it. What does the fifth wire carry, and in which direction?
questions.concept: Missing branch current at a junction
questions.why:
Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so the total entering equals the total leaving. Entering: 4.20 + 1.35 = 5.55 mA. Leaving so far: 2.60 + 0.95 = 3.55 mA. The fifth wire must carry the balance, 5.55 − 3.55 = 2.00 mA, and it must carry it out of the junction.

2.00 mA entering has the right size and the wrong direction, which would make 7.55 mA arrive and only 3.55 mA leave; 0.70 mA entering comes from treating 1.35 mA as a leaving current as well; 5.55 mA leaving forgets the two branches that already carry current away.

questions.q: At node b two currents are assumed to enter, I₁ and I₂, and one current I₃ leaves. The ammeters give I₁ = 1.340 mA and I₃ = 0.905 mA. What is I₂?
questions.concept: Sign of a branch current from KCL
questions.why:
With entering positive and leaving negative, the node equation is I₁ + I₂ = I₃, so I₂ = I₃ − I₁ = 0.905 − 1.340 = −0.435 mA. The minus sign is not an error: it says that the current in that branch runs opposite to the direction assumed for it, so it actually leaves the node.

+0.435 mA drops the sign and hides that reversal; +2.245 mA adds I₁ and I₃ instead of subtracting; −2.245 mA does the same with the sign flipped.

questions.q: Two branches feed a node. One is a 10 kΩ resistor across 9.0 V and the other a 5.0 kΩ resistor across 9.0 V, and both currents enter the node. What current leaves it?
questions.concept: Branch currents from Ohm's law and KCL at a node
questions.why:
Find each branch current from Ohm's law: 9.0/10 = 0.90 mA and 9.0/5.0 = 1.80 mA, since volts divided by kilohms gives milliamperes directly. KCL then gives the current leaving as 0.90 + 1.80 = 2.70 mA.

0.90 mA uses only the first branch; 0.60 mA treats the two resistors as being in series, 9.0/15; 1.35 mA averages the two branch currents instead of adding them.

questions.q: For one row of a circuit the current worked out from the equations is I₃ = 0.500 mA, and the third ammeter reads 0.530 mA. What is the percentage difference of the measured value from the computed one?
questions.concept: Percentage difference between computed and measured current
questions.why:
Percentage difference = (observed − reference)/reference × 100. The computed value is the reference, so (0.530 − 0.500)/0.500 × 100 = 0.030/0.500 × 100 = +6.00 %. The sign is positive because the measured current is the larger of the two.

−6.00 % reverses which value is being compared with which; +5.66 % divides by the measured value, 0.030/0.530, instead of by the reference; +0.06 % loses the factor of 100.

questions.q: A 9.0 V supply feeds a node through a 1.0 kΩ resistor. Three 3.0 kΩ resistors carry the current away from that node in parallel. Find the current entering the node and the current in each branch.
options: 4.5 mA into the node and 1.5 mA in each branch
9.0 mA into the node and 3.0 mA in each branch
2.25 mA into the node and 0.75 mA in each branch
0.90 mA into the node and 0.30 mA in each branch
questions.concept: KCL with identical parallel branches
questions.why:
Three equal 3.0 kΩ resistors in parallel give 3.0/3 = 1.0 kΩ. The total resistance is 1.0 + 1.0 = 2.0 kΩ, so the current from the supply is 9.0/2.0 = 4.5 mA. That current arrives at the node and splits equally between three identical branches, 4.5/3 = 1.5 mA each, and the three branch currents add back to 4.5 mA, as KCL requires.

9.0 mA ignores the 1.0 kΩ feeding resistor; 2.25 mA adds 3.0 kΩ instead of the parallel value 1.0 kΩ; 0.90 mA adds all four resistors as if they were in series.

questions.q: At a node the two entering currents are recorded as I₁ = 0.82 mA and I₂ = −0.4300 mA. Give the current leaving the node to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.concept: Significant figures in a sum of currents
questions.why:
KCL gives I₃ = I₁ + I₂ = 0.82 + (−0.4300) = 0.39 mA. In a sum the answer is limited by the reading with the fewest decimal places: 0.82 is given to two, so the result is quoted to two decimal places, 0.39 mA.

0.3900 mA and 0.390 mA claim four and three figures, which the 0.82 mA reading cannot support; 1.25 mA adds the magnitudes and throws away the minus sign, which would mean the branch feeds the node instead of draining it.

questions.q: A branch carries a steady current of 0.45 mA into a node for 2.0 minutes. How much charge enters the node in that time?
questions.concept: Charge carried by a steady current
questions.why:
Current is charge per unit time, so Q = It with I in amperes and t in seconds. I = 0.45 mA = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ A and t = 2.0 × 60 = 120 s, so Q = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 120 = 0.054 C = 54 mC. Charge conservation at the node is the reason Kirchhoff's First Law holds.

0.90 mC uses t = 2 s and never converts the minutes; 54 C leaves the current in milliamperes; 27 mC halves the answer, as if 2.0 minutes were 60 s.

questions.q: Why is an ammeter connected in series in the branch whose current it measures, rather than across a component in that branch?
options: It measures the potential difference across the branch
In parallel it would read the sum of all the branch currents
It must carry the whole of the branch current it measures
It has a high resistance, so it must not be placed across a component
questions.concept: Why an ammeter is connected in series
questions.why:
An ammeter responds to the current passing through it, so the only way it can read a branch current is to be part of that branch and carry all of it. It is built with a very low resistance so that inserting it barely reduces the current it is there to measure.

Measuring potential difference is the voltmeter's job; connected across a component the low-resistance ammeter would short that component out and read a large current set by the rest of the circuit, not the branch current; and a high resistance would be a reason to avoid series connection, which is why voltmeters are the ones placed in parallel.

questions.q: A single loop contains a 15 V supply and a 6.0 V supply connected so that they drive current the same way round, together with a 3.0 kΩ and a 4.0 kΩ resistor. What is the current in the loop?
questions.concept: Loop current with two aiding emfs
questions.why:
Around the loop the sum of the drops equals the sum of the emfs. The two supplies aid each other, so the total emf is 15 + 6.0 = 21 V, and the resistors are in the same loop, so they add to 7.0 kΩ. Then I = 21/7.0 = 3.0 mA, using volts divided by kilohms to give milliamperes.

1.29 mA subtracts the emfs, which is the answer for supplies connected in opposition; 2.14 mA uses the 15 V supply alone; 0.86 mA uses the 6.0 V supply alone.

questions.q: The second loop equation of a circuit is I₂R₂ − I₁R₅ + I₂R₁ = −E₂. With R₁ = 10 kΩ, R₂ = 1.0 kΩ, R₅ = 5.0 kΩ, E₂ = 9.0 V and I₁ = 1.100 mA, find I₂.
questions.concept: Solving a KVL loop equation for a branch current
questions.why:
Collect the I₂ terms: I₂(R₂ + R₁) = −E₂ + I₁R₅. The right-hand side is −9.0 + (1.100)(5.0) = −9.0 + 5.5 = −3.5 V, and R₂ + R₁ = 11 kΩ, so I₂ = −3.5/11 = −0.318 mA. The negative answer means the real current in that branch runs against the direction assumed on the diagram.

+0.318 mA drops the sign; −1.32 mA takes the I₁R₅ term across with the wrong sign, giving (−9.0 − 5.5)/11; −3.50 mA divides by R₂ alone and forgets that R₁ also carries I₂.

questions.q: A single loop contains a 24 V supply and resistors of 2.0 kΩ, 3.0 kΩ and 7.0 kΩ in series. Find the loop current and the potential difference across the 3.0 kΩ resistor.
questions.concept: Potential divider in a single series loop
questions.why:
The same current flows through all three resistors, so the total resistance is 2.0 + 3.0 + 7.0 = 12.0 kΩ and I = 24/12.0 = 2.0 mA. The drop across the 3.0 kΩ resistor is then IR = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 V. As a check, the three drops are 4.0, 6.0 and 14.0 V, and they add to the 24 V supplied, which is KVL.

8.0 V splits the 24 V equally between three unequal resistors; 12.0 mA uses only the 2.0 kΩ resistor; 4.0 V is the drop across the 2.0 kΩ resistor, not the 3.0 kΩ one.

questions.q: Two loop equations reduce to 10I₁ + 4I₂ = 10 and 5I₁ + 8I₂ = 2, with the currents in mA and the right-hand sides in volts. Find I₁ and I₂.
questions.concept: Solving two simultaneous loop equations
questions.why:
Double the second equation to 10I₁ + 16I₂ = 4 and subtract the first: 12I₂ = −6, so I₂ = −0.5 mA. Substituting back, 10I₁ = 10 − 4(−0.5) = 12, so I₁ = 1.2 mA. Check in the second equation: 5(1.2) + 8(−0.5) = 6 − 4 = 2.

+0.5 mA loses the sign, and the check then gives 10 rather than 2; the swapped pair puts each value in the other current's place and fails both equations; 1.0 mA with 0.0 mA comes from solving the first equation alone with I₂ assumed zero.

questions.q: In one loop the shared resistor R₅ = 5.0 kΩ carries 0.75 mA, and the loop is traversed in the direction opposite to that current. Give the size of the potential difference across R₅ and the sign its term takes in the loop equation.
questions.concept: Sign of a resistor term in a loop equation
questions.why:
The size is IR = 0.75 mA × 5.0 kΩ = 3.75 V, milliamperes times kilohms giving volts directly. The sign rule is that a potential difference across a resistance is positive when the resistance is traversed in the same direction as the current through it and negative otherwise, so here the term is −3.75 V. This is exactly why the shared resistor appears with opposite signs in the two loop equations, since the two loops pass through it in opposite senses.

Positive ignores the direction of travel; 6.67 V divides R by I; 0.15 V divides I by R.

questions.q: Walking once round a closed loop the potential drops across the resistors are 4.5 V, 2.8 V and 1.7 V. The loop contains a 12 V battery driving the current and a second battery of emf E opposing it. Find E.
questions.concept: Sum of voltage drops equals sum of emfs
questions.why:
KVL in the form used here says the sum of the drops around the loop equals the net emf in it. The drops total 4.5 + 2.8 + 1.7 = 9.0 V. Since the second battery opposes the first, the net emf is 12 − E, so 12 − E = 9.0 and E = 3.0 V.

9.0 V quotes the total drop and forgets that the 12 V battery is also in the loop; 21.0 V adds the two emfs as if they aided each other; 12.0 V ignores the opposing battery altogether.

questions.q: A DC supply of emf 9.0 V has an internal resistance of 0.50 kΩ and delivers 1.50 mA to a circuit. What potential difference appears across its terminals?
questions.concept: Terminal potential difference and internal resistance
questions.why:
The internal resistance is inside the loop, so it takes its own share of the emf: the lost volts are Ir = 1.50 mA × 0.50 kΩ = 0.75 V. The terminal potential difference is what is left, 9.0 − 0.75 = 8.25 V. This is one reason measured currents come out slightly below the values computed from the dialled emfs.

9.75 V adds the lost volts instead of subtracting them; 9.00 V treats the supply as ideal; 8.99 V takes the internal resistance as 0.50 Ω and is out by a factor of 1000.

questions.q: One of the circuit equations reads I₃R₃ + I₃R₄ + I₁R₅ = E₁. Which of Kirchhoff's laws does it express, and which conservation principle does that law rest on?
options: Kirchhoff's Current Law; conservation of charge
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law; conservation of charge
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law; conservation of energy
Kirchhoff's Current Law; conservation of energy
questions.concept: Telling a KVL equation from a KCL equation
questions.why:
Look at the units of the terms. Every term here is a voltage: three IR products and an emf. An equation in volts, written by going once round a closed path, is a Voltage Law equation, and the Voltage Law says that a charge carried right round a loop returns to the same potential, which is conservation of energy.

A Current Law equation is written at a single node and contains currents only, with no resistances and no emfs, for example I₁ + I₂ = I₃; it expresses conservation of charge. Pairing either law with the other's principle is the standard slip.

questions.q: A capacitor charges from zero through R = 10 kΩ with C = 470 μF from a 20 V supply. Take e⁻³ = 0.0498. What does the voltmeter across the capacitor read 14.1 s after the key is closed?
questions.concept: Capacitor voltage after a whole number of time constants
questions.why:
First the time constant: τ = RC = 1.0 × 10⁴ × 470 × 10⁻⁶ = 4.7 s, so 14.1 s is exactly 3τ. Then V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/τ)) = 20(1 − e⁻³) = 20(1 − 0.0498) = 20 × 0.950 = 19.0 V, the 95.0 % figure that belongs to three time constants.

1.0 V is 20e⁻³, the part of the rise still to come rather than the voltage reached; 12.6 V is 63.2 % of V₀, the value at one time constant; 17.3 V is 86.5 % of V₀, the value at two.

questions.q: A capacitor is charged through a 15 kΩ resistor. The voltmeter across it reaches 63.2 % of its final reading 33 s after the key is closed. What is the capacitance?
questions.concept: Capacitance from the time constant and R
questions.why:
The time to reach 63.2 % of the final voltage is the time constant itself, so τ = 33 s. From τ = RC, C = τ/R, with R converted to ohms first: C = 33/(1.5 × 10⁴) = 2.2 × 10⁻³ F = 2200 μF.

2.2 F leaves R in kilohms and is out by a factor of 1000; 455 μF computes R/τ instead of τ/R; 1390 μF takes 63.2 % of the time, 20.9 s, as the time constant, but 63.2 % applies to the voltage, not to the clock.

questions.q: Graphical analysis of a charging curve gives τ = 20.0 s with R = 10 kΩ. The capacitor is marked 2200 μF. Find the experimental capacitance and its percentage error.
questions.concept: Percentage error in an experimental capacitance
questions.why:
C = τ/R = 20.0/(1.0 × 10⁴) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ F = 2000 μF. Percentage error = (theoretical − experimental)/theoretical × 100 = (2200 − 2000)/2200 × 100 = 9.1 %, outside the 5 % this course treats as acceptable, which points at the capacitor's own tolerance or at leakage through the voltmeter.

10.0 % divides by the experimental value instead of the marked one; 0.091 % loses the factor of 100; 200 μF misplaces a decimal point in C and then carries the slip into the error.

questions.q: In an RC charging circuit the resistance is doubled and the capacitance is halved at the same time. What happens to the time constant and to the time taken to reach 63.2 % of the supply voltage?
options: τ doubles, so charging takes twice as long
τ halves, so charging takes half as long
τ is unchanged, so the time to reach 63.2 % is unchanged
τ is unchanged, but the final voltage doubles
questions.concept: Effect on the time constant of changing R and C
questions.why:
The time constant is the product τ = RC. Replacing R by 2R and C by C/2 gives τ = 2R × C/2 = RC, unchanged, and the time to reach 63.2 % of the supply voltage is exactly one time constant, so it is unchanged too.

τ would double if only R were doubled and halve if only C were halved; here the two changes cancel. The final voltage is set by the supply, not by R or C, so it cannot double.

questions.q: A capacitor charges from a 12 V supply through R = 4.0 kΩ with C = 500 μF. Find the current at the instant the key is closed and the initial gradient of the V against t curve.
questions.concept: Initial charging current and initial gradient
questions.why:
At t = 0 the capacitor is uncharged, so the whole 12 V is across the resistor and I = V₀/R = 12/4000 = 3.0 × 10⁻³ A = 3.0 mA. The time constant is τ = RC = 4000 × 500 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.0 s, and the tangent to the curve at the origin has gradient V₀/τ = 12/2.0 = 6.0 V/s. That tangent meets the line V = V₀ at exactly t = τ, which is the second way of reading τ off the graph.

3.0 A leaves R in kilohms; 24 V/s multiplies V₀ by τ instead of dividing; 2.0 V/s quotes τ itself as the gradient.

questions.q: A 470 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V. How much charge does it hold, and how much energy is stored in it?
questions.concept: Charge and energy stored on a capacitor
questions.why:
Q = CV = 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 12 = 5.64 × 10⁻³ C = 5.64 mC. Energy E = ½CV² = 0.5 × 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 144 = 3.38 × 10⁻² J = 33.8 mJ.

67.7 mJ forgets the factor of one half and quotes CV²; 39.2 μC divides C by V instead of multiplying; 3.38 mJ has the energy out by a factor of ten from a misplaced decimal point.

questions.q:
Voltmeter readings while a capacitor charges:
t (s): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
V (V): 0, 5.84, 8.84, 9.40, 11.17, 11.57
One reading does not fit the smooth rise. Which is it?
questions.concept: Spotting an outlier in a charging table
questions.why:
On a charging curve each successive gain in voltage must be smaller than the one before, because the current falls as V rises. The gains here are 5.84, 3.00, 0.56, 1.77 and 0.40 V. The 0.56 V step followed by a larger 1.77 V step breaks that pattern, so the reading at t = 30 s is the odd one. The curve through the other five points, with V₀ = 12 V and τ = 15 s, predicts about 10.38 V there.

The readings at 10, 40 and 50 s all sit on that same smooth curve and give decreasing gains, so none of them needs repeating.

questions.q: A charging capacitor is treated as fully charged after about 5τ rather than after 1τ. What justifies that convention?
options: At τ it has reached 36.8 % of V₀ and at 5τ 95 %
τ is the time to charge halfway and 5τ is five times that
At τ it has reached only 63.2 % of V₀, and 99.3 % at 5τ
At τ the charging current is zero and at 5τ it is greatest
questions.concept: Why a capacitor is taken as fully charged after 5τ
questions.why:
The rise V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/τ)) approaches V₀ but never quite reaches it. At one time constant the capacitor has taken on 63.2 % of V₀, which is nowhere near full, while at five it has 99.3 %, close enough that the remaining 0.7 % is inside the reading error of the voltmeter.

36.8 % is the figure for a discharging capacitor, the fraction that remains rather than the fraction gained; τ is not a half-life, since half charge is reached at about 0.69τ; and the charging current is greatest at the start and falls towards zero, not the other way round.

questions.q: In the capacitor charging experiment the voltmeter is read by hand every 10 s against a stopwatch. Which is the dominant random error?
options: Tolerance of the capacitor's marked value
Reaction time in starting the stopwatch and reading the meter together
questions.concept: Dominant random error in the RC charging experiment
questions.why:
The observer has to start the clock at the instant the key closes and then read the meter at the instant each 10 s mark passes. Both depend on human reaction time, which varies from reading to reading in either direction, so it scatters the points about the curve and is reduced by repeating the run and averaging, or by choosing R and C so that τ is comfortably longer than a reaction time.

Capacitor tolerance, lead resistance and temperature drift all push every reading the same way in a given run, so they are systematic: they shift the value of τ obtained rather than scattering the points around it.

questions.q:
A capacitor discharges through a resistor from V₀ = 9.00 V. The voltmeter is read every 10 s:

t (s):  0     10    20    30    40    50
V (V):  9.00  6.03  4.04  2.71  1.82  1.22

Read the time constant from this table, interpolating for the time at which V has fallen to 36.8 % of V₀.
questions.concept: Reading the time constant off a discharge table at 0.368V₀
questions.why:
36.8 % of 9.00 V is 3.31 V, which lies between the readings at 20 s (4.04 V) and 30 s (2.71 V). Interpolating, t = 20 + (4.04 − 3.31)/(4.04 − 2.71) × 10 = 20 + 0.73/1.33 × 10 = 25.5 s.

17.7 s interpolates for half of V₀ (4.50 V), which gives the half-life 0.693τ and not τ; 11.7 s uses 63.2 % of V₀, the fraction gained in charging rather than the fraction left in discharging; 30.0 s simply quotes the next tabulated time instead of interpolating between two of them.

questions.q: For a discharging capacitor the best-fit line of ln V against t passes through (5.0 s, 2.50) and (65.0 s, 0.70). The resistor in the circuit is 8.2 kΩ. What is the capacitance?
questions.concept: Capacitance from the gradient of a ln V against t line
questions.why:
Since ln V = ln V₀ − t/τ, the gradient is −1/τ. Gradient = (0.70 − 2.50)/(65.0 − 5.0) = −0.0300 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/(−0.0300) = 33.3 s and C = τ/R = 33.3/8200 = 4.07 × 10⁻³ F = 4.07 × 10³ μF.

3.66 μF takes the gradient itself as τ instead of inverting it; 4.07 F leaves R as 8.2 rather than 8200 Ω; the negative answer attaches the gradient's minus sign to τ, which is a time and cannot be negative.

questions.q: A capacitor discharges through a 220 kΩ resistor. The voltmeter falls from 12.0 V to 3.0 V in 40.0 s. What is the capacitance?
questions.concept: Time constant from two voltages on a decay
questions.why:
V = V₀e^(−t/τ), so 3.0/12.0 = 1/4 = e^(−40/τ) and 40/τ = ln 4 = 1.386. Hence τ = 40/1.386 = 28.9 s and C = τ/R = 28.9/220 000 = 1.31 × 10⁻⁴ F = 131 μF.

182 μF assumes the 40 s is one whole time constant, which would need V to fall to 4.41 V; 252 μF multiplies by ln 4 instead of dividing; 302 μF uses log₁₀4 = 0.602 in place of the natural logarithm.

questions.q: A 220 μF capacitor is discharged through a 150 kΩ resistor. How long does the voltage across it take to fall to half of its initial value?
questions.concept: Half-life of an RC discharge
questions.why:
τ = RC = 150 × 10³ × 220 × 10⁻⁶ = 33.0 s. Half voltage needs e^(−t/τ) = 0.5, so t = τ ln 2 = 0.693 × 33.0 = 22.9 s.

33.0 s quotes τ itself, which is the time to fall to 36.8 % and not to 50 %; 16.5 s halves τ, as though the time and the voltage fell in step; 47.6 s divides τ by 0.693 instead of multiplying by it.

questions.q: A 470 μF capacitor is charged until the voltmeter reads a steady 15.0 V. The key is then opened and it discharges. How much charge is still on it one time constant later?
questions.concept: Charge remaining after one time constant
questions.why:
Q = CV, so the fully charged capacitor holds Q₀ = 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 15.0 = 7.05 × 10⁻³ C = 7.05 mC. Charge decays on the same exponential as voltage, Q = Q₀e^(−t/τ), so after one time constant 36.8 % is left: 0.368 × 7.05 = 2.59 mC.

7.05 mC is the starting charge, before any decay; 4.46 mC is 63.2 % of it, the fraction a charging capacitor has gained rather than the fraction a discharging one still holds; 0.95 mC is 13.5 %, the value after two time constants.

questions.q: A discharge graph gives τ = 14.0 s for a circuit whose resistor is 6.8 kΩ. The capacitor is marked 2200 μF. What is the percentage error in the experimental capacitance?
questions.concept: Percentage error in an experimental capacitance
questions.why:
C = τ/R = 14.0/6800 = 2.06 × 10⁻³ F = 2059 μF. Percentage error = (theoretical − experimental)/theoretical × 100 = (2200 − 2059)/2200 × 100 = 6.4 %.

6.9 % divides by the experimental value instead of by the marked one, which is the reference; 93.6 % quotes the ratio 2059/2200 rather than the shortfall; 141 % takes the difference of 141 μF and calls it a percentage.

questions.q: The tangent drawn to a V against t discharge curve at t = 0 cuts the time axis at 24.0 s. The curve starts at V₀ = 9.60 V and the resistor is 12 kΩ. What are the initial gradient of the curve and the capacitance?
questions.concept: Time constant from the tangent at t = 0
questions.why:
The tangent at t = 0 cuts the time axis at exactly t = τ, so τ = 24.0 s. The initial gradient is −V₀/τ = −9.60/24.0 = −0.400 V/s, negative because the voltage is falling. Then C = τ/R = 24.0/12 000 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ F = 2.00 × 10³ μF.

The positive gradient forgets that a discharge curve descends; −2.50 V/s is τ/V₀, the reciprocal of the gradient; 2.00 μF slips three powers of ten in converting farads to microfarads.

questions.q: Two capacitors, 1000 μF and 470 μF, are charged to the same voltage and then discharged through separate 10 kΩ resistors, both keys opened at the same instant. At t = 10.0 s, what is the ratio of the voltage across the 1000 μF capacitor to that across the 470 μF one?
questions.concept: Comparing two RC discharges at the same instant
questions.why:
τ₁ = 10⁴ × 1000 × 10⁻⁶ = 10.0 s and τ₂ = 10⁴ × 470 × 10⁻⁶ = 4.70 s. The two voltages are V₀e^(−10/10.0) and V₀e^(−10/4.70), so the ratio is e^(−1.000 + 2.128) = e^1.128 = 3.09.

2.13 is just the ratio of the capacitances, which would be the answer only if voltage were proportional to C; 0.324 inverts the ratio and makes the slower capacitor the emptier one; 1.13 quotes the exponent without taking its exponential.

questions.q: A student measuring the discharge of a capacitor linearises the readings by plotting ln(V₀ − V) against t instead of ln V. What does that graph look like?
options: A straight line of gradient −1/τ, the same as ln V against t
A horizontal line, since V₀ − V stays constant
A curve, because ln(V₀ − V) is the linearisation for charging and not for discharging
questions.concept: Choosing the right linearising plot for charge and discharge
questions.why:
In a discharge V = V₀e^(−t/τ), so ln V = ln V₀ − t/τ is what gives the straight line. Forming V₀ − V gives V₀(1 − e^(−t/τ)), whose logarithm is ln V₀ + ln(1 − e^(−t/τ)) and is not linear in t, so the plot bends and has no single gradient. ln(V₀ − V) belongs to charging, where V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/τ)) makes V₀ − V the exponential quantity.

Both straight-line options assume one plot linearises either process; the horizontal line would need V to be constant, which is the one thing a discharge is not.

questions.q: In a J-tube the mercury stands level in both limbs and the trapped air column is 24.0 cm long at atmospheric pressure 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. The open limb is raised until the column has shortened to 18.0 cm. Take ρ(mercury) = 13 600 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 m/s². What is the level difference h?
questions.concept: Level difference from a Boyle's law compression
questions.why:
The bore is uniform, so volume goes with column length and P₂ = P₁ℓ₁/ℓ₂ = 1.013 × 10⁵ × 24.0/18.0 = 1.351 × 10⁵ Pa. The mercury supplies only the increase: ρgh = 1.351 × 10⁵ − 1.013 × 10⁵ = 3.38 × 10⁴ Pa. With ρg = 13 600 × 9.8 = 133 280 Pa per metre, h = 33 767/133 280 = 0.253 m = 25.3 cm.

101.3 cm forgets to subtract atmospheric pressure before dividing by ρg; 344.6 cm uses the density of water instead of mercury; 6.0 cm is the shortening of the air column, which is a tube length and not a level difference.

questions.q: A fixed mass of dry air occupies 25.0 ml when the mercury levels are equal and the pressure is 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. On a graph of P (y-axis, Pa) against 1/V (x-axis, m⁻³), what are the gradient and the intercept?
questions.concept: Gradient of P against 1/V
questions.why:
Boyle's law is PV = constant, so P = (PV) × (1/V) is a straight line whose gradient is the constant itself. PV = 1.013 × 10⁵ × 25.0 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 2.53 J, and the intercept is zero because P must vanish as 1/V does.

0.395 J⁻¹ is 1/PV, which is the gradient when the axes are the other way round; the 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa intercept confuses the starting pressure with an intercept, and a non-zero intercept would in fact signal a systematic error; 2.53 × 10⁶ J leaves the volume in millilitres.

questions.q: Trapped air in a J-tube stands at atmospheric pressure with the mercury level in both limbs. The open limb is then raised until its mercury stands 19.0 cm higher than in the closed limb. Taking atmospheric pressure as 76.0 cmHg = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa, what is the pressure of the trapped air?
questions.concept: Converting a mercury height to a gas pressure
questions.why:
The trapped air already stood at atmospheric pressure when the levels were equal, and the excess mercury column adds to that: P = 76.0 + 19.0 = 95.0 cmHg. Converting, P = 1.013 × 10⁵ × 95.0/76.0 = 1.27 × 10⁵ Pa.

2.53 × 10⁴ Pa is the 19.0 cm column on its own, leaving atmospheric pressure out; 7.60 × 10⁴ Pa subtracts the column instead of adding it; 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa ignores the raised limb altogether.

questions.q: The uniform bore of a Boyle's law tube has cross-sectional area 0.80 cm² and the trapped air column is 15.0 cm long. What value of 1/V goes on the graph, in m⁻³?
questions.concept: Volume of a trapped air column from its length
questions.why:
V = ℓA = 15.0 × 0.80 = 12.0 cm³ = 1.20 × 10⁻⁵ m³, so 1/V = 1/(1.20 × 10⁻⁵) = 8.33 × 10⁴ m⁻³.

6.67 × 10⁴ m⁻³ assumes a bore of 1 cm² and treats the 15.0 cm length as the volume; 8.33 × 10⁻² is 1/V left in cm⁻³, wrong by a factor of 10⁶; 1.20 × 10⁻⁵ is the volume itself and not its reciprocal.

questions.q:
Readings on a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature:

P (kPa):  101.3  114.6  128.0  141.3  154.6
V (cm³):  20.0   17.7   15.8   13.5   13.1

One reading does not fit Boyle's law. At which pressure was it taken?
questions.concept: Spotting an outlier by testing PV for constancy
questions.why:
Boyle's law says PV is constant, so form the product with P in pascals and V in cubic metres: 2.026, 2.028, 2.022, 1.908 and 2.025 J. Four of them agree to within 0.3 %, while the row at 141.3 kPa gives 1.908 J, nearly 6 % low, so that is the reading out of line.

The rows at 114.6, 128.0 and 154.6 kPa all reproduce the first row's product of 2.026 J, so none of them can be the odd one.

questions.q: 30.0 ml of dry air is trapped in a J-tube at 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa with the mercury levels equal. The open limb is raised until the level difference is 180 mm. Take ρ(mercury) = 13 600 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 m/s². What volume does the air now occupy?
questions.concept: Applying P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ after a pressure increase
questions.why:
ρgh = 13 600 × 9.8 × 0.180 = 2.40 × 10⁴ Pa, so P₂ = 1.013 × 10⁵ + 2.40 × 10⁴ = 1.253 × 10⁵ Pa. At constant temperature P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so V₂ = 30.0 × 1.013 × 10⁵/(1.253 × 10⁵) = 24.3 ml.

37.1 ml inverts the pressure ratio and lets a compressed gas expand; 126.7 ml uses ρgh alone as the new pressure and drops atmospheric pressure; 0.13 ml leaves h in millimetres, inflating ρgh by a factor of 1000.

questions.q: In one Boyle's law run the first row gives PV = 2.026 J and the last row gives PV = 2.145 J. What is the percentage difference of the last value from the first?
questions.concept: Percentage drift in the product PV
questions.why:
Percentage difference = (observed − reference)/reference × 100, taking the first row as the reference: (2.145 − 2.026)/2.026 × 100 = +5.9 %. The sign is positive because the product has drifted upward, which is what happens when a compressed gas is read before it has cooled back to room temperature.

+5.5 % divides by 2.145, the value being tested rather than the reference; −5.9 % reverses the subtraction and hides the direction of the drift; +11.9 % quotes the raw difference of 0.119 J as if it were already a percentage.

questions.q: A student computes the gas pressure as ρgh only, leaving atmospheric pressure out, and plots 1/V against P. Compared with the correct graph, what does that line look like?
options: The same gradient, but cutting the 1/V axis at a positive value
A steeper line still passing through the origin
A curve rising away from the origin
The same line, since only the labelling of the axis changes
questions.concept: Signature of an omitted constant pressure on the graph
questions.why:
Every pressure is short by the same amount, P_a, so every point slides the same distance to the left. Shifting a straight line sideways leaves its gradient untouched but destroys the zero intercept, and the line now cuts the 1/V axis at a positive value. A non-zero intercept is the standard sign of a systematic error in this experiment, and a forgotten atmospheric pressure is the commonest cause.

The gradient cannot change, since the same 1/V values are plotted against pressures all shifted by one constant; the points stay collinear, so no curve appears; and the numbers plotted really do change, so this is not a relabelling.

questions.q: A 120 g aluminium block of specific heat 900 J/kg·°C at 98.0 °C is dropped into 150 g of water (c_w = 4186 J/kg·°C) held in a 60.0 g copper calorimeter (c_c = 387 J/kg·°C), both at 21.0 °C. What is the final temperature of the mixture?
questions.concept: Final temperature of a mixture from heat lost equals heat gained
questions.why:
Heat lost by the solid equals heat gained by water and calorimeter: m_s c_s(T_s − T_f) = (m_w c_w + m_c c_c)(T_f − T_r). Here m_s c_s = 0.120 × 900 = 108.0 J/°C and m_w c_w + m_c c_c = 0.150 × 4186 + 0.0600 × 387 = 627.9 + 23.2 = 651.1 J/°C. Solving, T_f = (108.0 × 98.0 + 651.1 × 21.0)/(108.0 + 651.1) = 24 258/759.1 = 32.0 °C.

32.3 °C drops the calorimeter term, so the mixture appears to warm more than it does; 29.4 °C puts water's 4186 into the calorimeter term; 59.5 °C is the plain average of 98.0 and 21.0, ignoring both the masses and the specific heats.

questions.q: A 55.0 g aluminium calorimeter (c_c = 900 J/kg·°C) holds 120.0 g of water (c_w = 4186 J/kg·°C). When a hot block is dropped in, the mixture warms from 18.4 °C to 19.8 °C. How much heat have the water and the calorimeter together gained?
questions.concept: Heat gained by water and calorimeter together
questions.why:
The total heat capacity is m_w c_w + m_c c_c = 0.1200 × 4186 + 0.0550 × 900 = 502.3 + 49.5 = 551.8 J/°C. The rise is 19.8 − 18.4 = 1.4 °C, so Q = 551.8 × 1.4 = 773 J.

703 J leaves the calorimeter out, understating the heat gained; 69.3 J is the calorimeter's share on its own; 7.73 × 10⁵ J keeps the masses in grams against specific heats quoted per kilogram, an error of 10³.

questions.q: In one run the water and calorimeter together have a heat capacity of 320.0 J/°C, of which the calorimeter contributes 18.0 J/°C. A student leaves the calorimeter term out of the working equation. By what percentage is the computed specific heat of the solid then too low?
questions.concept: Effect of the omitted calorimeter term on c_s
questions.why:
c_s is directly proportional to the heat capacity in the numerator, so dropping 18.0 J/°C replaces 320.0 by 302.0. The computed value is 302.0/320.0 = 0.944 of the true one, that is 5.6 % too low.

6.0 % divides the missing 18.0 by 302.0, the reduced figure, instead of by the correct 320.0; 18 % mistakes 18.0 J/°C for a percentage; 94.4 % quotes the ratio itself rather than the shortfall.

questions.q: How much heat must be supplied to raise the temperature of 250 g of aluminium of specific heat 900 J/kg·°C from 22.0 °C to 95.0 °C?
questions.concept: Heat supplied from Q = mc∆T
questions.why:
Q = mc∆T with m = 0.250 kg and ∆T = 95.0 − 22.0 = 73.0 °C: Q = 0.250 × 900 × 73.0 = 1.64 × 10⁴ J.

2.14 × 10⁴ J uses the final temperature 95.0 °C as if it were the rise; 7.64 × 10⁴ J puts water's 4186 J/kg·°C in place of aluminium's 900; 1.64 × 10⁷ J leaves the mass in grams while the specific heat is per kilogram.

questions.q: The mixtures experiment is repeated several times and the heat gained by the water and calorimeter is plotted against the mixture's temperature rise. The line is straight through the origin with gradient 551.8 J/°C. The calorimeter is aluminium, 55.0 g, c_c = 900 J/kg·°C, and c_w = 4186 J/kg·°C. What mass of water does it hold?
questions.concept: Mass of water from the gradient of Q against ∆T
questions.why:
Q = (m_w c_w + m_c c_c)∆T, so the gradient is the total heat capacity, 551.8 J/°C. The calorimeter contributes 0.0550 × 900 = 49.5 J/°C, leaving 551.8 − 49.5 = 502.3 J/°C for the water, so m_w = 502.3/4186 = 0.120 kg = 120 g.

132 g forgets to remove the calorimeter's share; 144 g adds that share instead of subtracting it; 558 g divides the water's share by the calorimeter's specific heat rather than by water's.

questions.q: A mixtures run uses m_s = 12.0 g, m_w = 105.4 g and m_c = 44.2 g, and the mixture's temperature rise is 1.6 °C. The calculator returns c_s = 386.4271 J/kg·°C. How should the result be quoted?
questions.concept: Significant figures set by the least precise measurement
questions.why:
A computed result may carry no more significant figures than the least precise quantity it rests on. The three masses are given to 3 significant figures, but the temperature rise, 1.6 °C, carries only 2, and it multiplies straight into the numerator. So c_s is good to 2 significant figures: 3.9 × 10² J/kg·°C.

386 and 386.4 keep 3 and 4 figures, more than a rise of 1.6 °C can support; quoting all seven digits claims a precision that a thermometer read to 0.1 °C cannot deliver.

questions.q: A 45.0 g block at 96.0 °C is dropped into 90.0 g of water at 20.0 °C in a 50.0 g copper calorimeter (c_c = 387 J/kg·°C). The mixture settles at 23.7 °C. Take c_w = 4186 J/kg·°C. Accepted specific heats: aluminium 900, iron 450, copper 387, lead 128 J/kg·°C. Which metal is the block?
questions.concept: Identifying a metal from its measured specific heat
questions.why:
m_w c_w + m_c c_c = 0.0900 × 4186 + 0.0500 × 387 = 376.7 + 19.4 = 396.1 J/°C, and the rise is 23.7 − 20.0 = 3.7 °C, so the heat gained is 1466 J. On the solid's side m_s(T_s − T_f) = 0.0450 × (96.0 − 23.7) = 3.254 kg·°C, so c_s = 1466/3.254 = 450 J/kg·°C, which is iron.

Aluminium at 900 would have delivered about twice the heat and about twice the temperature rise; copper's 387 is the calorimeter's value here, not the block's; lead at 128 would barely have moved the thermometer.

questions.q: A little hot water from the beaker is carried over on the block into the calorimeter. What does this do to the computed specific heat of the solid?
options: Nothing, because the carried water joins water that has already been weighed
It makes it too low, since a film of water cools the block on the way
It makes it too high, since heat from that water is credited to the block
Nothing, because m_w and T_f are both raised in the same proportion
questions.concept: Effect of water carried over on the block
questions.why:
The working equation credits every joule gained by the water and calorimeter to the block alone. The carried water arrives at roughly 95 °C and gives up heat of its own, so T_f ends higher than the block by itself could have produced. The numerator is inflated while m_s(T_s − T_f) is not, so c_s comes out too high.

The carried water was never on the balance, so it is not part of the weighed m_w; it is hotter than the mixture, so it warms rather than cools it; and there is no proportionality between the extra mass and the extra temperature that would let the two effects cancel.

questions.q: A student's arithmetic returns a negative value for the specific heat of the solid. Which single mistake produces that?
options: The calorimeter term was left out of the heat gained
The masses were left in grams while the specific heats are per kilogram
Water's specific heat was used for the calorimeter
The solid's temperature drop was written as (T_f − T_s)
questions.concept: Sign checks on the temperature differences
questions.why:
In c_s = (m_w c_w + m_c c_c)(T_f − T_r)/[m_s(T_s − T_f)] both differences must be positive, because T_s > T_f > T_r always holds. Writing the denominator as (T_f − T_s) reverses one of them and puts a minus sign on the whole result. A negative specific heat is physically impossible, so it is a reliable signal that a temperature difference has been subtracted backwards.

Omitting the calorimeter, or using the wrong specific heat in it, changes the size of the answer but never its sign; leaving the masses in grams changes it by a factor of 1000, again with the sign intact.

questions.q: The needle of a tangent galvanometer settles 38.0° from its undeflected position when a bar magnet is placed end-on beside it. Take the Earth's horizontal flux density as B_H = 40 × 10⁻⁶ T. What is the flux density of the magnet's field at the needle?
questions.concept: Applying the tangent law B = B_H tan θ
questions.why:
The needle sits in two perpendicular horizontal fields and settles along their resultant, so B = B_H tan θ = 40 × 10⁻⁶ × tan 38.0° = 40 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.781 = 31.3 × 10⁻⁶ T.

51.2 μT divides by the tangent instead of multiplying, which is the field belonging to the complementary angle; 24.6 μT uses sin 38.0° in place of tan 38.0°; 40.0 μT quotes B_H itself, which the magnet's field would equal only at a deflection of 45°.

questions.q: A graph of tan θ_AV against d/(d² − L²)² is a straight line through the origin of gradient s = 0.0250 m³. Take B_H = 36 × 10⁻⁶ T and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. What is the magnetic dipole moment of the bar magnet?
questions.concept: Magnetic moment from the gradient of the tangent-law graph
questions.why:
The working equation is tan θ = (μ₀/4π)(2M/B_H) · d/(d² − L²)², so the gradient is s = μ₀M/(2πB_H) and M = 2πB_H s/μ₀. Since 2π/μ₀ = 5 × 10⁶, M = 5 × 10⁶ × 36 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.0250 = 4.50 A·m².

2.25 A·m² drops the factor 2 and uses πB_H s/μ₀; 9.00 A·m² doubles instead; 5.65 × 10⁻⁶ A·m² treats 36 × 10⁻⁶ as a field strength in A/m and computes 2πH₀s, giving an answer six orders of magnitude too small.

questions.q: A bar magnet 12.0 cm long lies end-on with its centre 0.30 m from the needle of a tangent galvanometer, and the needle deflects 40.0°. Take B_H = 40 × 10⁻⁶ T and μ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T·m/A, with B = (μ₀/4π) · 2Md/(d² − L²)². What is the magnetic dipole moment?
questions.concept: Magnetic moment from a single end-on deflection
questions.why:
L is the half-length, 0.060 m, so d² − L² = 0.0900 − 0.0036 = 0.0864 m², (d² − L²)² = 7.465 × 10⁻³ m⁴ and d/(d² − L²)² = 40.19 m⁻³. The tangent law gives B = 40 × 10⁻⁶ × tan 40.0° = 3.356 × 10⁻⁵ T. Then M = B/(2 × 10⁻⁷ × 40.19) = 3.356 × 10⁻⁵/(8.038 × 10⁻⁶) = 4.18 A·m².

3.20 A·m² takes L as the full 12.0 cm rather than the half-length; 4.53 A·m² uses the point-dipole form 2M/d³, which holds only when d is much greater than L; 8.35 A·m² drops the factor 2 in 2Md.

questions.q: For a bar magnet of full length 10.0 cm observed end-on at d = 0.30 m, by what percentage does the exact field 2Md/(d² − L²)² exceed the point-dipole field 2M/d³ for the same magnet?
questions.concept: Exact end-on field against the point-dipole approximation
questions.why:
The two expressions differ only in the denominator, so their ratio is d⁴/(d² − L²)² = [d²/(d² − L²)]². With L = 0.050 m, d² = 0.0900 m² and d² − L² = 0.0875 m², so the ratio is (1.0286)² = 1.0580 and the exact field is 5.8 % larger.

2.9 % forgets to square and quotes d²/(d² − L²) − 1; 11.9 % squares the ratio twice; 5.5 % divides the excess by the exact value rather than by the approximation being compared with it.

questions.q:
Readings for a 10.0 cm bar magnet, with L the half-length:

d (cm):     45      40      35      30
tan θ_AV:   0.2726  0.3889  0.6068  0.7813

The graph of tan θ_AV against d/(d² − L²)² should be a straight line through the origin. At which distance is the reading inconsistent with the other three?
questions.concept: Testing a line through the origin by constant ratio
questions.why:
For a line through the origin the ratio tan θ_AV ÷ d/(d² − L²)² must be the same at every distance. With L = 0.050 m the abscissae are 11.25, 16.12, 24.31 and 39.18 m⁻³, so the ratios are 0.0242, 0.0241, 0.0250 and 0.0199 m³. The first three agree to about 3 %, while the value at 30 cm is nearly 20 % below them, so that reading is out of line.

The readings at 45, 40 and 35 cm all give a gradient near 0.0244 m³, so none of them can be the odd one.

questions.q: The magnetic moment is computed with the Earth's horizontal flux density taken as the nominal 40 × 10⁻⁶ T, but the true local value is 33 × 10⁻⁶ T. What is the error in the computed moment?
questions.concept: Propagating the error in B_H into M
questions.why:
M = 2πB_H s/μ₀ is directly proportional to B_H, so an overstated field gives an overstated moment in the same proportion: M_computed/M_true = 40/33 = 1.212, that is 21 % too high.

21 % too low reverses the direction of an overestimate; both 18 % answers divide the 7 × 10⁻⁶ T difference by the nominal 40 instead of by the true 33, which is the wrong reference for a percentage error.

questions.q: Used in its original role as a current meter, the same instrument obeys tan θ ∝ I. A current of 0.50 A deflects the needle 30.0°. What current gives a deflection of 45.0°?
questions.concept: Tangent law with current in place of the magnet
questions.why:
Since tan θ is proportional to I, I₂ = I₁ tan θ₂/tan θ₁ = 0.50 × tan 45.0°/tan 30.0° = 0.50 × 1.000/0.5774 = 0.87 A.

0.75 A treats the angle itself as proportional to the current and scales by 45/30; 0.29 A multiplies by tan 30.0° instead of dividing; 1.00 A assumes 45° always means unit current, which is true only when the two fields happen to be equal.

questions.q: The metre stick is laid north to south, so the magnet lies broadside-on to the needle rather than end-on. Which expression then gives the magnet's flux density at the needle?
questions.concept: End-on and broadside-on fields of a bar magnet
questions.why:
Broadside-on, the needle lies on the perpendicular bisector of the magnet, so both poles are the same distance √(d² + L²) away and their fields add as vectors instead of subtracting along the axis. The result carries a plus sign and a three-halves power: (μ₀/4π) · M/(d² + L²)^(3/2).

2Md/(d² − L²)² is the end-on expression the experiment normally uses; 2M/d³ is its far-field limit; the last option mixes the broadside power with the end-on minus sign and describes neither position.

questions.q: A single circular loop of radius 0.15 m is to produce a flux density of 8.00 μT at its centre. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. What current must it carry?
questions.concept: Current from the flux density at the centre of a loop
questions.why:
At the centre of a single loop B = μ₀I/2R, so I = 2RB/μ₀ = 2 × 0.15 × 8.00 × 10⁻⁶/(1.2566 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.91 A.

0.955 A drops the factor 2; 3.82 A applies it twice; 6.00 A uses B = μ₀I/2πr, which belongs to a long straight wire and not to the centre of a loop.

questions.q: A single-turn loop of radius 0.12 m carrying 1.80 A is replaced by a 20-turn coil of the same radius carrying the same current. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. What does the tesla meter read at the centre?
questions.concept: Field at the centre of a multi-turn coil
questions.why:
For one turn B = μ₀I/2R = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.80/0.240 = 9.42 × 10⁻⁶ T. Every turn contributes the same field at the centre, so B = μ₀NI/2R and the reading is 20 × 9.42 = 189 μT.

9.42 μT is the single-turn value and forgets N, which is exactly the trap in a formula that contains no N; 377 μT also drops the 2 in 2R; 0.471 μT divides by N instead of multiplying.

questions.q: On the axis of a single circular loop, what percentage of the flux density at the centre is left at an axial distance equal to the loop's own radius?
questions.concept: Axial fall-off of the field of a circular loop
questions.why:
B(z) = μ₀IR²/[2(R² + z²)^(3/2)] and B(0) = μ₀I/2R, so B(z)/B(0) = R³/(R² + z²)^(3/2). Putting z = R gives R³/(2R²)^(3/2) = 1/2^(3/2) = 0.354, that is 35.4 %.

50.0 % uses R²/(R² + z²) and forgets the three-halves power; 25.0 % squares that ratio; 12.5 % cubes it, applying the power to the wrong quantity.

questions.q: The best-fit line of B against the factor IR²/[2(R² + z²)^(3/2)] has gradient 1.19 × 10⁻⁶ H/m. Taking the accepted permeability of free space as 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m, what is the percentage error?
questions.concept: Percentage error in a measured value of μ₀
questions.why:
The gradient of that plot is μ₀ itself. The accepted value is 4π × 10⁻⁷ = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ H/m, so the error is (1.19 × 10⁻⁶ − 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶)/(1.2566 × 10⁻⁶) × 100 = −5.3 %, that is 5.3 % low.

5.6 % low divides by the measured gradient instead of by the accepted value, which is the reference; 5.3 % high reverses the sign and claims the measurement exceeds the accepted figure; 0.067 % low quotes the raw difference of 0.067 × 10⁻⁶ as though it were already a percentage.

questions.q: A single loop of radius 0.20 m carries 1.50 A and the Hall probe sits on the axis 0.15 m from the centre. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. What reading is expected on the tesla meter?
questions.concept: Axial flux density of a current-carrying loop
questions.why:
R² + z² = 0.0400 + 0.0225 = 0.0625 m², and (0.0625)^(3/2) = 0.015625 m³. The plotted factor is IR²/[2(R² + z²)^(3/2)] = 1.50 × 0.0400/(2 × 0.015625) = 1.92 A/m, so B = μ₀ × 1.92 = 2.41 × 10⁻⁶ T = 2413 nT.

4712 nT is the value at the centre, z = 0; 603 nT omits the three-halves power and uses (R² + z²) itself; 11 170 nT uses the far-field form μ₀IR²/2z³, which needs z much greater than R and is badly wrong here where z is smaller than R.

questions.q: Two single loops carry the same current. Loop A has radius 0.080 m and loop B has radius 0.20 m. What is the ratio of the flux density at A's centre to that at B's centre?
questions.concept: Dependence of the central field on loop radius
questions.why:
At the centre B = μ₀I/2R, so with the current fixed B is inversely proportional to R. B_A/B_B = R_B/R_A = 0.20/0.080 = 2.5, so the ratio is 2.5 : 1 and the smaller loop has the stronger field.

1 : 2.5 makes B proportional to R instead of inversely proportional; 6.25 : 1 and 1 : 6.25 square the radius ratio, which belongs to the R² of the axial formula and cancels at the centre.

questions.q: Why is the whole run repeated with coils of several different radii?
options: To find the radius at which the central field is largest
To cancel the Earth's field, which reverses when the radius changes
To hold the tesla meter on one range while the current is varied
To confirm that the gradient is the same whatever the radius, as it must be for a constant of free space
questions.concept: Why the loop radius is varied
questions.why:
The gradient of B against the computed factor is μ₀, a property of free space and of nothing in the apparatus. If the method is sound, coils of different radii must all yield the same gradient, so repeating with several radii is the test of that claim and also gives independent values to average.

The central field simply rises as R falls, so no radius maximises it; the Earth's field does not depend on the coil and is not cancelled by changing R; and the meter's range is set by the size of B, not by how many coils are used.

questions.q: The Hall probe is clamped at a small fixed angle to the axis instead of parallel to it, and stays that way all through the run. What happens to the graph of B against the computed factor?
options: The points scatter randomly with no systematic shift
Every reading is low, so the gradient and the value of μ₀ come out too small
The line keeps its gradient but gains a positive intercept
Every reading is high, so μ₀ comes out too large
questions.concept: Effect of a misaligned Hall probe on the gradient
questions.why:
A Hall probe reads only the component of the field along its own sensitive direction. A fixed tilt multiplies every reading by the cosine of that angle, a number less than one, so all the points drop by the same factor. The line stays straight and still passes through the origin, but its gradient, which is the measured μ₀, is too small.

A fixed tilt is systematic and does not scatter the points; a constant multiplying factor tilts the line rather than shifting it, so no intercept appears; and a component of a vector can never exceed the vector, so the readings cannot come out high.

questions.q: A rod of uniform cross-sectional area 4.0 mm² carries an axial tensile force of 120 N. What is the tensile stress in the rod?
questions.concept: Tensile stress from force and cross-sectional area
questions.why:
Stress = F/A with the area in square metres: 4.0 mm² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², so σ = 120/(4.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 3.0 × 10⁷ Pa, or 30 MPa.

30 Pa leaves the area in mm²; 3.0 × 10⁴ Pa converts millimetres to metres once instead of squaring the conversion factor; 3.3 × 10⁻⁸ Pa computes A/F, the reciprocal of the stress.

questions.q: A steel wire 1.50 m long is under a tensile stress of 8.0 × 10⁷ Pa. Its Young modulus is 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. What are the strain and the extension?
questions.concept: Strain and extension from stress and Young modulus
questions.why:
E = stress/strain, so strain = σ/E = 8.0 × 10⁷/(2.0 × 10¹¹) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴, a pure number with no unit. Extension = strain × original length = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 1.50 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.60 mm.

0.40 mm quotes the strain in millimetres and never multiplies by the length; the 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ pairing multiplies by 1.50 twice, once in the strain and once again in the extension; 2.5 × 10³ divides E by the stress and gives a strain no wire could survive.

questions.q: A beam of rectangular cross-section has breadth b = 25.0 mm and thickness d = 8.0 mm. What is its second moment of area, I = bd³/12?
questions.concept: Second moment of area of a rectangular section
questions.why:
Convert first: b = 0.0250 m and d = 0.0080 m. Then d³ = 5.12 × 10⁻⁷ m³ and I = 0.0250 × 5.12 × 10⁻⁷/12 = 1.07 × 10⁻⁹ m⁴.

1.04 × 10⁻⁸ m⁴ puts the cube on the breadth, db³/12, which is the stiffness for bending the beam the other way round; 1.28 × 10⁻⁸ m⁴ forgets to divide by 12; 1.07 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ leaves the breadth in millimetres.

questions.q: A copper beam of Young modulus 1.20 × 10¹¹ Pa spans 0.90 m between two mounts. Its breadth is 30.0 mm and its thickness 10.0 mm, and a 400 g load hangs at the centre. Take g = 9.8 m/s². What is the central depression, Y = mgℓ³/(4Ebd³)?
questions.concept: Central depression of a loaded beam
questions.why:
Numerator: mgℓ³ = 0.400 × 9.8 × 0.90³ = 0.400 × 9.8 × 0.729 = 2.858. Denominator: 4Ebd³ = 4 × 1.20 × 10¹¹ × 0.0300 × (0.0100)³ = 1.44 × 10⁴. So Y = 2.858/(1.44 × 10⁴) = 1.98 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.198 mm.

0.0165 mm keeps the 48 of Y = mgℓ³/48EI after already substituting I = bd³/12, so it divides by 12 twice; 0.245 mm fails to cube the span; 198 mm leaves the load in grams.

questions.q: Two beams of identical span, breadth and thickness are loaded at the centre. The aluminium beam gives a Y against m line of gradient 1.18 × 10⁻³ m/kg and the copper beam 0.680 × 10⁻³ m/kg. The Young modulus of the aluminium is 69 GPa. What is the Young modulus of the copper?
questions.concept: Comparing Young moduli from two gradients
questions.why:
The gradient is s = gℓ³/(4Ebd³), so when the span, breadth and thickness are the same, s is inversely proportional to E and the product Es is the same for both beams. E_Cu = E_Al × s_Al/s_Cu = 69 × 1.18/0.680 = 120 GPa, and the stiffer metal does give the shallower line.

40 GPa inverts the ratio and makes the shallower line belong to the softer metal; 69 GPa treats the modulus as a property of the shape rather than of the metal; 208 GPa squares the ratio of the gradients.

questions.q: In a repeat run the span between the mounts is halved and the thickness of the beam is halved as well, with the breadth, the load and the metal unchanged. By what factor does the central depression change?
questions.concept: Scaling the depression with span and thickness
questions.why:
Y = mgℓ³/(4Ebd³), so Y goes as ℓ³ and as 1/d³. Halving the span multiplies Y by 1/8; halving the thickness multiplies it by 8. The two cubes cancel exactly, so the depression is unchanged.

One eighth follows the shorter span alone and forgets that a thinner beam sags more; eight times follows the thinner beam alone; one sixty-fourth multiplies the two eighths together instead of dividing.

questions.q: A beam's thickness is recorded as 10.0 mm when its true value is 9.5 mm, every other quantity being exact. By what factor is the computed Young modulus wrong?
questions.concept: Propagating a thickness error into E
questions.why:
E = gℓ³/(4bd³s), so E depends on 1/d³ and an overstated thickness gives an understated modulus. E_computed/E_true = (9.5/10.0)³ = 0.857, so the result is 14 % too low. This is why the thickness is measured with a micrometer at several points: a 5 % slip in d becomes a 14 % slip in E.

0.950 leaves the ratio uncubed; 0.815 raises it to the fourth power; 1.166 inverts the ratio and turns a thickness measured too large into a modulus that comes out too large.

questions.q: During a run the loads are increased until the beam no longer returns to its unloaded reading when the masses are taken off. What does the graph of Y against m then show?
options: The points stay on the line but its gradient doubles
The points scatter randomly about the line at every load
The points bend away from the straight line at the largest loads
The line stays straight but cuts the Y axis below the origin
questions.concept: Effect of exceeding the proportional limit
questions.why:
The straight line through the origin exists only while stress stays proportional to strain, that is below the proportional limit. Once that limit is passed the beam takes a permanent set, each further kilogram buys more than its share of depression, and the points at the top of the range curve away from the line drawn through the small loads.

A doubled gradient would move every point, not just the heavy ones; the departure is systematic and repeatable, not random scatter; and a line cutting below the origin is the mark of a dial gauge that was never zeroed, which shifts the light loads too.
